basis: New mission, no workbook source; authored per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. Facts and sources: NHI single-payer system began 1995, near-universal coverage, run by 衛福部中央健康保險署 (NHI Administration). Premium rate held at 5.17% since 2021, confirmed unchanged for 2025 and 2026 by the NHI committee (全民健康保險會, Nov 2024 meeting; UHO/HakkaNews Nov 2025 coverage), vs South Korea ~7% and Japan ~10%. Safety reserve (安全準備金) projected at ~2.1-2.2 months of benefit payments at end of 2025 per the Nov 2024 committee meeting (mohw.gov.tw cp-4624 series; wantrich.chinatimes.com 2026-05-09 coverage of Minister 石崇良). Taiwan crossed 20% 65+ population in 2025 (467.3万, 20.06%), officially a "super-aged society" per Ministry of Interior data (CNA 2026-01-09 reports; 14% threshold reached 2018). Old-age dependency ratio ~27 per 100 working-age residents in 2025 (moi.gov.tw statistical bulletin); longer-range ~2 working-age adults per elderly by 2040 cited via globaltaiwan.org/Brookings commentary — kept general, not stated as a precise official figure. National medical-expenditure long-range projection (~NT$1.3 trillion circa 2020 rising several-fold by mid-century) from a government science-policy forecast (cited via ctee.com.tw), kept in general terms per playbook guidance since the multiple is approximate. Health spending ~6.6-6.9% of GDP vs OECD ~9.7%, Japan ~10.6%, South Korea ~8.4%, US ~17% (mohw.gov.tw national health expenditure report; twreporter.org OECD comparison piece). NHI total annual budget passed NT$800 billion circa 2022 (mohw.gov.tw cp-5020-63299). Health Bank (健康存摺) ~12 million users, several hundred million data views, now linking Google/Apple/Garmin wearable data via SDK (mohw.gov.tw cp-16-79026 Google/NHI Administration release). "AI-on-DM" partnership with Google and National Health Research Institutes announced 2024 to predict type-2 diabetes complications, planned to extend to other chronic diseases (blog.google zh-tw 2024 Cloud Summit Taipei release; taiwan-healthcare.org coverage; cohesiondata.com news). Family-medicine/大家醫計畫 integrated-care clinics described only in general terms ("thousands of clinics") since an exact current count was not confirmed. No partisan cross-strait framing used. Register and structure per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md; calibration matched to content/authored/levels/sdg13-1.*.json.

slides.1: Most of us carry an NHI card without ever asking what actually keeps it funded. It pays for doctors, medicine and dental care whenever we need them. So can Taiwan realistically keep affording it?
slides.2: SDG 3 sets one global objective: good health and well-being for the body and the mind together. Taiwan pursued something close to this for three decades, long before that particular name existed.
slides.3: Taiwan's National Health Insurance has run as one unified plan since 1995. It now covers almost every resident on this crowded island. That is why health systems abroad have studied it for decades.
slides.4: Taiwan officially became a super-aged society in 2025, with one resident in five now 65 or older. That share has climbed from just 14 percent only seven years earlier. It keeps rising every year.
slides.5: As the population ages, medical spending keeps climbing right along with it. Experts expect health costs to grow much bigger in the decades ahead. Older patients simply need more medical care, more often than not.
slides.6: Here is the part that should worry you. The premium rate has not moved since 2021, even as costs keep increasing around it. Meanwhile, the safety reserve supporting the whole system keeps shrinking.
slides.7: NHI has covered nearly everyone in Taiwan since 1995, and that achievement has now held for three decades. Very few countries have matched this level of coverage so far.
slides.8: Taiwan spends a noticeably smaller share of its economy on health care than Japan, South Korea or the United States. Yet it still delivers broad coverage with low out-of-pocket costs. Few systems manage that combination.
slides.9: The NHI Administration has built a digital Health Bank that lets citizens view their own medical records online. Millions of people already use it. It can now pull in data from smartwatches too.
slides.10: Policymakers face a genuine trade-off here. They can raise the premium rate directly, or they can widen the base of income it is collected from. Neither option avoids making somebody in this country unhappy.
slides.11: One promising fix is catching illness earlier, through family doctors who track patients over time. That beats only treating people once they arrive at a hospital in crisis. Early care is simply cheaper.
slides.12: The NHI Administration has begun testing AI models, built with partners including Google, that scan health records for early warning signs. The goal is prevention, well before a disease becomes serious.
slides.13: Here is the risk, stated in the plainest possible terms. If the safety reserve keeps shrinking, it will eventually breach the level regulators require it to hold. The government would then have to act quickly.
slides.14: If premiums do rise, that cost will not be distributed evenly across everyone. Young workers and new graduates already earn the least of anyone in the system. A higher rate would affect them the most severely.
slides.15: Some argue Taiwan should simply match Japan's or South Korea's higher premium rate. However, a bigger number alone will not explain why expenses keep climbing. Taiwan also needs to reform how care is delivered.
slides.16: The clock is not on Taiwan's side, either. Large numbers of workers are retiring right now, which steadily diminishes the paying population year by year. The reserve needs them at the worst conceivable moment.
slides.17: So where does that leave us? NHI remains one of Taiwan's genuine achievements, yet it is also carrying real structural strain that has only grown heavier with each passing year.
slides.18: This is not an abstract discussion happening somewhere else. It is your card, your future premium and the care your own family will need. That already means you have a genuine stake in how this ends.
slides.19: Students in STEM fields have real tools to offer here. They can interpret data honestly, build better prediction models, or simply know the trade-offs well enough to argue for one clearly. That matters too.
slides.20: Taiwan has built something genuinely rare: broad coverage at a fair price for almost everyone. Let's work to keep it that way. What happens over the next three decades depends on the choices we make today.
